Beck.et: From Middle Low German beck, probably through Dutch bek, from Middle Dutch bec, from Middle French bec (“beak”) or Old French bec, from Vulgar Latin beccus, probably from Gaulish. Compare modern French bec, English beak.

s: a cylindrical or slightly conical drinking vessel without a stem, typically with no handle, beaker
Becher.et: From Middle High German bëcher, from Old High German bëhhâri, from Proto-West Germanic *bikārī. Displaced native Stauf in Early New High German. Cognate with English beaker.
From Middle High German bëcher, from Old High German bëhhâri, from Proto-West Germanic *bikārī. Displaced native Stauf in Early New High German. Cognate with English beaker.

s: a swimming pool or other artificial pool
a basin, large hollow, enclosed valley
Becken.et: From Middle High German becken, from Old High German becki, beckin, from Vulgar Latin *baccīnum (possibly attested as bacchinon, 6th century), probably from Gaulish. Compare Dutch bekken and further French bassin, English basin.

s: a common surname originating as an occupation
Becker.et: From Beck (“baker”) (from Middle High German becke), or a variant spelling of southern German Bäcker (“baker”).

s: A glass beaker, flat-bottomed vessel fit for liquids

Beckmann.et: In some cases probably from Middle Low German bēke (“brook”), frequently spelt becke, compare -beck; thus a doublet of the also common name Bachmann. In other cases it may be from Beck (“baker”).

s: Placename suffix found in northern Germany
-beck.et: From Middle Low German bēke, from Old Saxon beki, from Proto-West Germanic *baki. Doublet of -bach.

Béchamelsauce.et: Partial calque of French sauce béchamel, made from French béchamel + Sauce.

Beckmesser.et: Figurative sense after the character Sixtus Beckmesser in Richard Wagner's opera Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg (1867).
